sentences.text: Shastasaurus was a reptile that lived during the Triassic period.
This animal had a very slender profile, with a ribcage less than 2 meters high despite a trunk flipper distance of nearly 7 meters.
It possessed an unusually short skull with a blunt, toothless snout, which was distinct from the elongated, toothed dolphin-like snouts of most other ichthyosaurs.
Shastasaurus sikanniensis had a ribcage less than 2 meters deep despite a flipper-to-flipper distance of over 7 meters.
It is unknown whether Shastasaurus possessed a dorsal fin, though the basal ichthyosaur Mixosaurus did.
The upper tail fluke of Shastasaurus was likely much less developed than the shark-like tails found in later ichthyosaur species.
If Shastasaurus sikanniensis is correctly classified within the genus, it would be the largest species, reaching 21 meters in length.
The largest specimen of Shastasaurus liangae measures 8.3 meters in length.
A juvenile specimen of Shastasaurus liangae was found measuring approximately 3.74 meters in length.
The type species of Shastasaurus is S. pacificus, which lived during the late Carnian period in northern California.
S. pacificus is known only from very fragmentary remains, leading to the assumption that it was a 'normal' ichthyosaur with standard body proportions, especially in the skull.
S. sikkanniensis was originally described in 2004 as a giant species of the genus Shonisaurus.
In 2009, Shang and Li reclassified the species Guizhouichthyosaurus tangae as Shastasaurus tangae.
There are 10 recorded fossil occurrences of the genus Shastasaurus in the Paleobiology Database.
The part of the Shastasaurus skull containing the jaw-opening muscles was particularly large, and the animal had large hyoid bones that allowed it to pull its tongue back abruptly.
The short snout suggests Shastasaurus was likely a suction feeder that ate mainly soft-bodied cephalopods lacking shells for defense.
Shastasaurus likely created a sudden water flow to suck prey into its open mouth by rapidly opening its jaws and pulling its tongue back.
Shastasaurus has been interpreted as a specialized predator of fish and shell-less cephalopods that hunted using suction.
Shastasaurus liangae was the first species to definitively show that Shastasaurus was an animal with distinctive short snouts and toothless jaws.
The parent group and the family of the genus Shastasaurus are both Shastasauridae.
However, later analyses showed that Guizhouichthyosaurus was actually more closely related to advanced ichthyosaurs and cannot be considered a species of Shastasaurus.
Doubtful species referred to this genus include S. carinthiacus from the Austrian Alps and S. neubigi from the Muschelkalk in Germany.
The genus Shastasaurus lived from the Carnian to the Norian periods, between 237 and 205.7 million years ago.
Fossils of Shastasaurus have been discovered in the United States, Canada, and China.

Current research suggests Shastasaurus jaws may not have been adapted for suction feeding because their hyoid bones were unsuitable for impact forces and related species possessed teeth and gut contents indicating a different diet.
A 2013 discovery of a juvenile specimen suggested that Guanlingsaurus (formerly Shastasaurus liangae) should be considered a distinct genus due to its shorter hyoid bone.
The classification of Shastasaurus sikanniensis remains debated, with analyses in 2013, 2019, and 2021 yielding conflicting results regarding its relationship to Shonisaurus versus Shastasaurus.
